title: Marcus' blind spots
hook: Christians were persecuted in his reign, and he made his son Commodus heir: admiration and honesty together

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last words of the Meditations, the actor leaving the stage at peace. Your line was go gladly. Did you end the day on purpose? This week we finished book twelve: fate, two gates, opinion, forgetting, a small share, depart content. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

We've just spent more than a hundred days inside one man's notebook. We've heard him talk himself out of anger, into kindness, toward death without fear. It's easy, after that long, to start treating him like a saint. But Marcus Aurelius was also a Roman emperor, with an emperor's power, for nineteen years. And two facts from his reign sit uneasily beside the notebook. The path doesn't skip them. Today: Commodus, held next to everything we admire.
screen: `A HUNDRED DAYS IN HIS NOTEBOOK.` → `ALSO AN EMPEROR, NINETEEN YEARS.` → `TWO UNEASY FACTS.`

segments.voice: First, the Christians. During Marcus's reign, Christians were put to death in several places. Around the year 165 in Rome, the teacher Justin was tried and executed. The judge was the city prefect, Junius Rusticus, the same Rusticus whom Marcus thanks in book one for lending him the works of Epictetus. In 177, in Lyon in Gaul, a group of Christians were tortured and killed, a story preserved by the church historian Eusebius. Historians debate how much Marcus directed any of this. There was no single empire-wide order, and much was local. But it happened under his rule, and some cases reached him. The Meditations mention Christians once, briefly and coldly, and even that line may have been added by a later hand. Second, Commodus. For most of the century before Marcus, emperors had passed power to adopted heirs chosen for ability, partly because they had no surviving sons. Marcus had one, and made him co-emperor in 177. When Marcus died in 180, Commodus ruled for twelve years, and ancient historians remember those years as cruel and chaotic. Third, what to do with this. Not to throw the notebook away, and not to explain the facts away. The man who wrote about kinship with every human mind also governed an empire that killed people for their faith. Both are true. Fourth, why it matters for us. Every person we admire, a teacher, a parent, a hero, comes with blind spots. Learning from someone doesn't require pretending they had none.
screen: `JUSTIN AND LYON: DEATHS IN HIS REIGN.` · `COMMODUS, A SON AS HEIR.` · `DON'T DISCARD, DON'T EXCUSE.` · `EVERY HERO HAS BLIND SPOTS.` · then, large: `BOTH AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you admire, living or dead, someone close or someone famous. Let yourself feel what you admire in them. Now, gently, let one of their failings come into view too, something real. Notice the urge to push one of these away, either the admiration or the failing. Try not to. Hold both at once, side by side, like two stones in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Commodus. The son Marcus made co-emperor, remembered by ancient historians as cruel and chaotic once he ruled alone. Today's word.
Your line: both at once. When you catch yourself making someone all good or all bad today, add the other half back in. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Many modern readers of the Meditations read them alongside the history of Marcus's reign, including the persecution of Christians and the succession of Commodus.

match.prompt: Marcus' blind spots. tap the pairs.
pairs: Christian teacher executed in Rome, c. 165
the judge, and Marcus's own teacher

myth: Marcus issued a single empire-wide order to persecute Christians
historians find no such order; much was local, though it happened under his rule.
the judge at Justin's trial was Rusticus, whom Marcus thanks in book one
the same Rusticus who lent him Epictetus.
before Marcus, several emperors in a row had chosen adopted heirs
Marcus, with a surviving son, made Commodus co-emperor in 177.

fork.setup: you've loved a teacher's book for months. then you learn about something wrong done on their watch. what does the path suggest?
options: keep both the admiration and the honesty.
fork.reveal: the path keeps the notebook and the history together. both are true of Marcus, and of most people we admire.

trapdoor: what you thought: Marcus was the good emperor, a philosopher-king.
what it means: a real man, whose notebook teaches kinship, and whose reign saw Christians killed and a cruel heir chosen.

what a scholar hears: Justin's Acts name Junius Rusticus as judge, Eusebius preserves the letter on the martyrs of Lyon and Vienne, and the single reference to Christians in Meditations 11.3 is often suspected to be a gloss.

sources.ref: The Martyrdom of Justin (Acts of Justin)

notes: Justin Martyr's trial before the urban prefect Q. Junius Rusticus, usually dated c. 162–168; confirm 'around 165'. Confirm this Rusticus is the one in Meditations 1.7 (most scholars accept it).
Martyrs of Lyon and Vienne, 177, in the letter preserved by Eusebius, Church History 5.1. Confirm date.
Meditations 11.3: the phrase about Christians is suspected by many editors to be a later gloss. Confirm hedge.
Marcus reigned 161–180 (nineteen years). Commodus made co-Augustus 177, sole emperor 180–192 (twelve years). Confirm.
Adoptive succession: Nerva to Trajan to Hadrian to Antoninus to Marcus, partly because those emperors lacked surviving sons. Hedged; confirm.
The Christian door may want a Keeper to check the framing of the martyrdoms; it states facts without ranking anyone.
